title: Multi-dimensional spectroscopy of mobile excitons in two-dimensional semiconductors
authors: Ned Wheaton, Jeffrey A. Davis, Jesper Levinsen, Meera M. Parish
abstract: Multi-dimensional coherent spectroscopy (MDCS) goes beyond standard linear-response probes and provides a powerful tool for investigating correlations between quasiparticles such as excitons (bound electron-hole pairs). Here we present a microscopic theory of MDCS that accounts for the delocalized nature of excitons in two-dimensional semiconductors. In contrast to the more phenomenological few-level approaches typically employed for modelling MDCS, our theory features mobile excitons with continuous momentum degrees of freedom. We find that the energy continuum associated with exciton momenta is crucial for producing interaction-induced decoherence, as well as capturing the interference between different exciton-polaron quasiparticles in the case of charge-doped semiconductors. Crucially, our calculated MDCS spectra agree well with recent experiments on doped monolayer MoSe$_2$ [Hao et al., Nature Communications 8, 15552 (2017)], and they suggest that the interactions between exciton polarons depend strongly on phase-space filling effects, where exciton polarons compete for electrons. Our results demonstrate that microscopic approaches allow one to gain new insights from the fine structure of MDCS on two-dimensional semiconductors, and they illustrate the utility of microscopic approaches to modelling MDCS experiments more generally.
summary: This work presents a microscopic theory for Multi-dimensional Coherent Spectroscopy (MDCS) applied to excitons in 2D semiconductors. By incorporating the continuous momentum of excitons, the theory captures complex interaction effects like decoherence and phase-space filling. The results provide a strong theoretical framework validated against recent experimental data on MoSe2.
main_problem: To develop a microscopic theory for Multi-dimensional Coherent Spectroscopy (MDCS) that accurately models the delocalized nature of excitons in two-dimensional (2D) semiconductors, moving beyond simple phenomenological models.
main_result: The theory successfully predicts MDCS spectra that quantitatively agree with experiments on doped monolayer MoSe2, highlighting the crucial role of exciton momentum continuum and phase-space filling effects.
method: The authors use time-dependent perturbation theory to calculate the nonlinear optical response, focusing on the third-order polarization ($P^{(3)}$) to probe higher-order correlations.
model_or_system: The system involves excitons (bound electron-hole pairs) in 2D semiconductors, modeled microscopically to account for continuous momentum degrees of freedom and interactions with doping-induced polarons.
key_observables: MDCS spectra, specifically the third-order response, which reveals signatures of interaction-induced decoherence and phase-space filling.
important_parameters: Exciton momentum continuum, doping concentration, and the coupling strength of the optical field ($\hat{V}(t)$).
main_assumptions: The theory relies on time-dependent perturbation theory and makes approximations regarding the initial state (pure state) and the dipole moment operator.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the phase control mechanisms in MDCS using pulse ordering, frequency shifts, and wavevector differences, and show Feynman diagrams for rephasing and double quantum pathways.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from general MDCS theory (linear response) to modeling mobile excitons, culminating in a detailed, advanced model incorporating doping and polaron interactions in MoSe2.
why_interesting: The detailed microscopic treatment of coherent spectroscopy in low-dimensional materials provides powerful tools for understanding many-body dynamics, correlation effects, and quasiparticle interactions in solid-state quantum optics.
